attacker.model: claude (Kiro subagent; exact model version not exposed to the agent)

null-vs-empty.notApplicableReason: The only parameter is one nvarchar(1000) JSON document; NULL vs '' (NULL document inserts nothing without error, '' fails ISJSON) is exercised by named cases on the payload, not by a typed text column the trap checker inspects.

collation-case.notApplicableReason: Case sensitivity of the stored VehicleRegistration is exercised by a named case ('WWI-A' vs an existing 'wwi-a' row); the rego value itself is a JSON token inside the string argument, not a typed text column.

dates-datetime.notApplicableReason: The datetime boundary is a 'when' token inside the JSON string (covered by a named case), not a typed date column or a cutoff window the trap checker reads.

numeric-rounding.notApplicableReason: The decimal rounding is a 'temp' token inside the JSON string (covered by the 3.965 case), not a typed decimal column the trap checker reads.

top-ties.notApplicableReason: The procedure inserts rows parsed from one JSON document and reads no table for row selection, so there is no two-row tie in a typed input to construct; array order within the document is covered by the parsing cases.

cases.label: a trailing space after the JSON object: still valid JSON, so the recording is inserted
cases.reasoning: The nvarchar(1000) argument ends in a space. ISJSON ignores trailing whitespace and the conversion's IS JSON test does too, so the single recording must still be parsed and inserted on both engines.

cases.label: duplicate 'temp' key: the first (1.5) wins; the second is in exponent notation (1e2)
cases.reasoning: OPENJSON ... WITH takes the first of duplicate keys. The hand-derived duplicate-key case repeats 'rego' (text); here the repeated key is the decimal 'temp', and its second value 1e2 is one the procedure rejects. SQL Server stores 1.50; a conversion that took the last value (jsonb, or ORDER BY ... DESC) would read 1e2 and raise.

cases.label: temperature -3.965 rounds half away from zero to -3.97 (half-up gives -3.96)
cases.reasoning: CAST of -3.965 to decimal(18,2) rounds the midpoint away from zero, to -3.97. The hand-derived case is the positive 3.965, where half-up and half-away-from-zero agree; for a negative midpoint, rounding half up (floor(x * 100 + 0.5)) gives -3.96 and banker's rounding gives -3.96.

cases.label: boundary datetime 9999-12-31 in 'when'
cases.reasoning: A 'when' of 9999-12-31T23:59:59.999999 is parsed by to_datetime2 and stored in datetime2(7)/timestamp; the maximum date tests the mapping's microsecond rounding against SQL Server's tick resolution.

cases.label: registration whose name differs only in case from an existing row
cases.reasoning: VehicleRegistration is stored verbatim; 'WWI-A' is inserted alongside an existing 'wwi-a' row. No case folding on either engine, so both rows remain distinct in Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures.

cases.label: the document is the JSON literal null (text 'null', not SQL NULL): not an object or array, so ISJSON is 0 and the call raises
cases.reasoning: ISJSON(N'null') is 0 because, without a type argument, ISJSON accepts only an object or an array; the procedure then throws. The hand-derived NULL-document case sends SQL NULL, for which ISJSON is NULL and nothing happens, and the hand-derived scalar case uses a different scalar. A conversion that tested 'IS JSON' (which accepts any JSON value) would go on to parse it and insert nothing without an error.

cases.label: temperature in upper-case exponent notation with a negative exponent (25E-1) is rejected
cases.reasoning: The procedure accepts a temperature only as plain decimal text; 25E-1 is valid JSON and equals 2.5, but SQL Server's conversion to decimal(18,2) refuses exponent notation and the call fails. A conversion that cast through numeric or float, or a pattern that allowed an exponent (any case, any sign), would store 2.50.

cases.label: two recordings, the first with an empty 'when' (1900-01-01) and the second dated normally: both inserted
cases.reasoning: An empty 'when' converts to 1900-01-01 00:00:00 on SQL Server (an empty string is not NULL); the second recording has a normal date. A conversion that mapped '' to NULL would store NULL or fail; the hand-derived case has a single recording, so this also checks that the empty-string branch applies per recording. The null-vs-empty trap is not claimed: the only text input is the document itself.

cases.label: a 1007-character argument whose first 1000 characters are a valid document followed by spaces: truncated to nvarchar(1000), it is valid and inserted
cases.reasoning: The parameter is nvarchar(1000), so SQL Server keeps the first 1000 characters: the document and trailing spaces, without the 'garbage' that follows. The truncated text is valid JSON and the recording is inserted. A conversion that did not truncate would see invalid JSON and raise. The hand-derived over-length case has the opposite outcome (truncation makes the JSON invalid).

objections.text: The hand-derived duplicate-key case sends the same first and second rego values and already requires OPENJSON-compatible first-occurrence behavior. A02 repeats that input and mechanism.
objections.resolution: A02 now duplicates the numeric temp key rather than rego, and makes the second occurrence exponent notation that would fail if selected. It tests first-occurrence handling through a distinct typed conversion path.

objections.text: The hand-derived temperature-rounding case already sends temp 3.965 in the same document shape and requires 3.97. A03 is the same attack with only the registration changed.
objections.resolution: A03 now sends -3.965. The negative midpoint distinguishes half-away-from-zero (-3.97) from half-up and half-even (-3.96), unlike the positive hand-derived midpoint.

objections.text: The hand-derived NULL-document case already calls the procedure with a NULL argument and requires no error and no inserted rows. A06 is identical.
objections.resolution: A06 now sends the JSON scalar text 'null', not SQL NULL. SQL Server ISJSON without a type constraint rejects that scalar, exposing a conversion that accepts all JSON values.
